verses.verse:
स्वासाधीनः स्वरालापो लयावपे तु मात्रिकः।
लयान्तरेण विश्रामो मुक्त तानेषु जायते।१२७।
verses.text: In svarālāpa the rest depends on the breath; in layālāpa it is measured in mātrās (beats); in mukta tānas the rest comes about through changes of laya (tempo).

commentary.text: That is, in svarālāpa the pause or rest taken on the nyāsa note depends on the breath of the singer or player and is of irregular duration. But when, after svarālāpa, we come to layālāpa (ālāpa in rhythm), that same rest comes to be based on a regular time, a self-chosen laya (tempo). For example, in ālāpa it goes Sa – – – – – – and in layālāpa Sa Sa Sa Sa. But when mukta tānas (free tānas) are composed, the amount of rest becomes less, and special tempos such as double and triple speed (do gun, tīn gun) are brought in. Then, when that same mukta tāna is weighed out to a regular count according to the tāla, we call it a baddha tāna (bound tāna). When one has come to know a rāga well, if the actions described above are done in that rāga one after another, the rāga shines, and through much practice the sādhaka (practitioner) begins to handle the form of that rāga without effort. Then absorption (tanmayatā) comes, and absorption itself becomes the path to happiness and peace for the sādhaka; and, as one liberated while living (jīvan-mukta), he becomes most beautiful for others as well. Our forebear Śrī Vedavyāsa ji wrote this very thing, making it a saying of Bhagavān Śrī Kṛṣṇa:

subsection.title: Rāga Vṛndāvanī Sāraṅg, Layālāp and Free Tānas
